Dandled
DAN-dld
verb
The past participle of dandle, of uncertain origin, akin to the Italian dandolare, “to dandle, to trifle”; to move a little child up and down upon the knee or in the arms in play and fondness. A KJV hapax.

Biblical Definition

To dandle is to bounce a little child gently upon the knee — the tender, playful, wholly unnecessary fondness of a mother with an infant who is already fed and already safe. The word occurs once in Scripture, at the very close of Isaiah, in the LORD’s last great promise to Zion: “Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the glory of the Gentiles like a flowing stream: then shall ye suck, ye shall be borne upon her sides, and be dandled upon her knees” (Isa 66:12). The figure is Jerusalem as a mother and her restored people as her nursing children, satisfied with the breasts of her consolations (Isa 66:11), carried on the hip, bounced on the knee. And then the LORD applies it to Himself in a simile: “As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you; and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem” (Isa 66:13). This is one of the most tender sentences in the prophets. God does not merely pardon His people, provide for them, and dismiss them; He comforts them as a mother comforts — the same word He uses when He says of Israel, can a woman forget her sucking child? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee (Isa 49:15). The Shepherd who gathers the lambs with His arm carries them in His bosom (Isa 40:11). The God whose peace comes like a river stoops to dandle His children on His knee.

Webster 1828 Definition

Dandled: bounced gently upon the knee, as a mother plays with an infant. A KJV hapax, in the LORD’s promise of motherly comfort to Zion.

DANDLE, to move a little child up and down in the arms or on the knee.

To fondle, to play with an infant in tenderness.

Of uncertain origin; akin to the Italian dandolare, “to dandle.”

A KJV hapax, occurring only as the participle dandled (Isa 66:12).

In Isaiah, the restored people are dandled upon the knees of Zion.

Key Scripture

Isa 66:12 — "For thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the glory of the Gentiles like a flowing stream: then shall ye suck, ye shall be borne upon her sides, and be dandled upon her knees."

Isa 66:13 — "As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you; and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem."

Isa 49:15 — "Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee."

Isa 40:11 — "He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young."

Modern Corruption

The live corruption is the feminist reimagining of God as Mother built on Isa 66:13; the text gives a comparison, not a name, and a simile is not a title.

expand to see more

There is a live corruption here, and it must be named. Isa 66:13 — “As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you” — has been made the chief proof-text of the feminist theology that would rename God as Mother, address Him as She, and recast the Fatherhood of the first Person as a cultural accident of an ancient people rather than revelation. The text will not bear it, and the reason is grammar before it is doctrine. Isaiah does not say God is a mother. He says God comforts as a mother comforts. That is a simile, a comparison of one action to another, and a comparison is not a name. Scripture compares the LORD to a lion, an eagle, a rock, a moth, a bear robbed of her whelps, a husbandman, a refiner’s fire; no one proposes that we address Him as Rock or pray to our Eagle in heaven. The whole prophecy is drenched in the point: the same verse says the comfort will be given “in Jerusalem,” and no one argues from that phrase that God is a city.

The corrective is to let Scripture set its own titles. God has named Himself, and He has done it with unwavering consistency: the LORD, the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ; and the Son taught His disciples to pray “Our Father, which art in heaven,” not to choose their own address for the Almighty. The pronouns Scripture uses of God are masculine from Genesis to Revelation, and the eternal relations of Father and Son are not borrowed from human sociology — human fatherhood is named from His, not He from ours. To rename God is not to enrich our devotion; it is to worship a god of our own making, which is idolatry however tender the motive. And nothing whatever is lost by refusing it. The Father who will not be called Mother is the very One who says He will comfort us as a mother comforts, extend peace to us like a river, carry us in His bosom, and dandle us upon His knees. The doctrine is not cold. It is only true.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means to bounce or fondle a little child upon the knee or in the arms.

Dandle — of uncertain origin, akin to Italian dandolare, “to dandle.”

It denotes moving an infant up and down on the knee in fondness and play.

A KJV hapax, occurring only as the participle dandled (Isa 66:12).

In Isaiah, Zion’s children are borne on her sides and dandled on her knees.

The LORD likens His comfort to a mother’s — a simile, not a name (Isa 66:13).

Usage

"Ye shall be borne upon her sides, and be dandled upon her knees — Zion’s nursing children."

"As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you: a comparison, not a title."

"The God who extends peace like a river stoops to dandle His children on His knee."
